newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark to host Rushdie despite security fears.
newsitem.headline: Denmark to host Rushdie despite security fears.

text.p: Denmark said on Friday British author Salman Rushdie would come to collect a literary prize next week, despite earlier government warnings that it could not guarantee to protect him from a possible assassin.

Indian-born Rushdie has lived in hiding and under guard since 1989 when Iranian revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a fatwa or death sentence against him for his novel "The Satanic Verses", saying it blasphemed against Islam.

Danish opposition politicians, who in the past few days came close to overthrowing the minority government over its admitted mishandling of the affair, said they were pleased but would go ahead with a full-scale debate next week at which parliament is likely to give Premier Poul Nyrup Rasmussen a stiff rebuke.
"It's great. But what remains to parliament is to examine the government's remarkable handling of this matter," opposition Liberal spokesman Anders Fogh Rasmussen said.

A joint statement by the Danish Rushdie Committee, the Culture Ministry and Cultural Capital '96 said Rushdie and other winners of European Union awards would receive their prizes at a ceremony in Copenhagen on November 13.
Conservative spokesman Per Stig Moeller welcomed the decision but said it came too late to save his country from international ridicule.
"Denmark has already become a laughing-stock," he said.
The government last week told Rushdie he could not attend a planned November 14 prizegiving because advance publicity of the event created an excessive security risk.
That decision, and the impersonal way in which it was conveyed to Rushdie in a press statement, angered the writer and brought howls of outrage from intellectuals and the media at home and abroad.

The exact location of next Wednesday's awards is not yet known, not because of secrecy but because the venue has not yet been chosen, organisers say. Attendance will be limited to specially-accredited journalists and about 500 invited guests.
There has so far been no explanation of how a November 14 visit could have been too dangerous, while a November 13 appearance -- now accompanied by far more publicity -- is deemed acceptable.

The initial government attempt to block the visit, and its somewhat woolly subsequent explanations, led some politicians to suspect Rasmussen was bowing to Iranian pressure, causing parliament's leftist fringe to consider joining a right-wing move for a vote of no confidence.

Socialist People's Party leader Holger Nielsen only came out in support of the centre-left government after intelligence briefings convinced him it had merely bungled rather than pursued a hidden political agenda.
The affair may yet land parliamentary justice commitee chairman Bjoern Elmquist in jail.

After attending a Wednesday session of the assembly's intelligence oversight committee, he told journalists that the original government attempt to keep Rushdie out was based on a specific threat to his safety rather than general concern.
That prompted other members of the forum, known familiarly as "the hush-hush committee" to complain that he had breached its secrecy rules and to threaten to bring charges against him.
